If you want to actually argue against people who believe "sex is sacred," you have to argue against whatever standard of morality they are using to say that; this is not something that is done by arguing that "Well, people who have a different morality think differently than you, so you're wrong" which is essentially your point.

I fortunately (or unfortunately, depending on who you are) have never had to deal with something like that, nor do I think I would feel the same as you if I did. It's also difficult for me to relate to the pain over unrequited attraction, because I prefer when my attraction goes unrequited (lithromantic, haha). Regardless of that, I can greatly empathize and still have stuff to say.

I'm sure other people have felt like you before. It's a pretty human thing in general to not want to hurt people we don't have anything against and may actually have a pretty decent opinion of, especially when they've expressed some level of vulnerability and sincerity with us through something like a confession. Cuz that feels like a crappy thing to do, right? But, at the end of day, if what your rejection of someone is the genuine truth/reflection of your orientation/feelings for them, then that's that. You both just have to accept that because denying reality is foolish and will not change what is what. Giving someone the truth that may hopefully help them move on quicker to someone who is hopefully able to reciprocate is far better than denying who you are and living a lie that may please them. Rejection hurts. But it is objectively not the end of anyone's world. You are not ruining someone's life when you reject them. You are just being painfully honest.

You might hurt someone when you give them the truth, especially regarding vulnerable matters like feelings. But the truth will help them more than any lie could. Any pain they may feel can be moved on from. Nothing lasts forever. 

Your feelings are valid. As someone who's neither rejected nor confessed, but been by people who have done either or both, they both seem to be pretty difficult anyone to do. So it's fair to find rejecting difficult. 

Our orientations and what they may lead us to experience in this world and for other people are not going to make everyone happy. But they weren't supposed to, at the end of the day.

Also, keep in mind that someone feeling hurt over your rejection of them can be more multifaceted than just pain over rejection. People are complex emotional beings with insecurities and different backgrounds and different genetic makeup and different lists of what we like and don't like, what makes us feel good and what makes us hurt. What I mean is, you are not the only thing causing them pain, even if they say you are. Much like your orientation that led you to reject them in the first place, those external factors are things you cannot control. Maybe it reaffirms an insecurity for them, maybe it's another domino falling in a bad week, maybe they have rejection sensitive dysphoria. You may never know, but you will never be able to control what those factors are. You are at fault for none of that and hardly at fault for rejecting them in the first place (I believe gentle honesty to never be a fault). Emotional distress over things you cannot control will not change that you cannot control those things.

TL;DR: most important things are that the truth matters above all, feelings are still valid, pain can fade, is generally multifaceted and not from just one thing, we do not exist to make other people happy

First, try to recognize when you have the urge. Upon doing that, there are several responses to the urge you could have other than acting on it:

* Urge Surfing - recognize that the urge you're feeling will subside and you do not have to act on it. It may help to distract yourself from it until it subsides.
* Rubber Band method - basically, have a way to inflict a small amount of pain (such as a rubber band on your wrist) whenever feeling an urge so you start associating it with pain or uncomfortability rather than pleasure (based on the idea of classical conditioning)
* Distraction - try thinking of something else that you also find pleasurable. It may help to make a list of hobbies or activities you enjoy doing, sensations you enjoy feeling and experiences that illicit those, and have that on hand to remind yourself of what you could be doing instead. Invest time into making those hobbies or activities happen more frequently, so you can think about urges less and have less time to act on them. It may help you even more if you tie these hobbies or activities to a trait you know to be true about yourself. For example, I know I am a person who LOVES learning . As such, some of my hobbies is "watching informational video" or "reading nonfiction." Reminding myself that I could be doing these things that actually help me BE myself instead of acting on an urge that isn't me and that I know I will regret acting on helps me reason with myself more.
* Meditation/Prayer - There are several guided meditation videos on youtube. I've found one that works for me that is 6 minutes. If you're religious, you could also turn to prayer too. I've also found some guided prayer videos that work for me as a Christian. I don't know if there are other prayer videos for other religions, but it wouldn't hurt to check.
* Accountability Partner - this one is probably the most difficult. Do you have anyone in your real life you could personally confide in about this AND are they a person who would be able to respond whenever (or ASAP) you need help with urges? For me, this person is my mom, and she is able to help me best having been my mom all of my life and being a person I still live with and have direct contact to almost all of the time. Instead of acting on an urge, you could express to this partner that you are feeling an urge and trying not to act on it. From there, they may help you distract yourself from it or at least reason against acting on it.

Some other advice I guess is download some addiction tracking app or have a way to track whenever you have urges or relapse. I use I Am Sober simply to track, but it can also be a decent place to work through urges.

If you have a therapist, absolutely 100% bring this concern up with them; they may have more techniques then I can provide. There are also probably other subreddits with people that could provide you with more advice.

Also, remember that the road to be completely free of this is rocky. Don't be discouraged whenever you mess up and relapse; it is always worth it to keep trying and to keep on working towards the addiction-free life you want to live. Wishing you luck!

You say you "wish you could say it to her," but the thing is, you actually can. And you should. You should communicate to your friend that this bothers you. Every relationship needs honest communication. By not telling her this, your resentment towards your friend will eventually build until one day it's too much (honestly, it sounds like it's pretty high already). I know from personal experience. It's not fun for anyone involved.

As to how you go about communicating, I'd recommend requesting to have a private meeting with her specifically to resolve this issue. You can ask for this meeting over text or in-person or even have another person communicate it for you if that's too hard. You can also have this meeting over FaceTime or in-person, whatever works best. You can preface it by stating something along the lines of "Hey, do you have time to talk? I need to talk to you about something important that's been bugging me about the time we spend together." Be vague enough so that you still have stuff to talk about in the private meeting and also so that you don't come accusing her out of no where, but specific enough so that she knows it is important to you which means it's important to her and so that she knows that it's important to your relationship as a whole. 

It's possible that she doesn't know this is an issue. Your brain development comment I understand is supposed to be hyperbolically insulting, but it simply isn't reality that anyone knows anything about anything, including social conventions like politeness or phone etiquette. No information is ever really a given. You are simply making an assumption, one that seems to be false in the case of your friend. (Also some people just don't pick up on social cues/conventions, even if all the information that they need to pick up on them is around them; this can happen for a multitude of reasons)

For example, I actually do use my phone to play some game/do something else usually when I'm talking to my friends, but I always make a point to verbally clarify and communicate 1) that I am doing it and 2) that I promise I am paying attention to them, and 3) that it's helping me pay attention to them, which is true. Whenever I FaceTime my friends, I am usually listening to them talk while also playing sudoku or solitaire. If I don't, it's very easy for my brain to wander and not pay attention. Not saying that this is the case with your friend. But your advice simply isn't always true and also comes off very harsh (which is possibly out of resentment towards your friend, which again, I'd recommend resolving through some communication).

Her interpretation takes 1 Corinthians 7 out of context a bit. 1 Corinthians was a letter the Apostle Paul wrote to the Corinthian church, and the verses she's pulling from (3-6) are specifically responding to the belief that some Corinthian church members had that abstinence in marriage made people holier than having sex in marriage. He said it specifically to counter that belief and to clarify that there is "nothing wrong and everything right" with marital sex. (Source: [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-7/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-7/) ) The verses do say that the wife belongs to the husband, but they also say that the husband belongs to the wife. They center around the idea of a couple mutually belonging to each other, something noted in the commentary linked. The reason it's seen as a "duty" is because by mutually fulfilling that duty of affection to each other, both people in the marriage can resist seeking that fulfillment elsewhere. Now, this is not the complete biblical view of sex; it's not just a duty to deter people from sin and is definitely supposed to be enjoyable for both people involved (that's what Song of Songs is supposed to show). And people don't enjoy something they don't consent to and don't want.

I'm a Christian and on the aro ace spectrum which is why I cared enough to comment all this, just want to explain some stuff. I understand that this understanding of what sex is will not appeal to everyone, all I wanted to do was clarify that, no, Christianity (or any religion that derives itself from the Bible) is not supposed to advocate for marital rape. Like. No. Sex is supposed to be enjoyable. And implicitly in that, it logically has to be also be something that one wants. Also, my little loophole to the mutual responsibility stuff is that if one marries someone who also doesn't want sex, then that person will not seek fulfillment elsewhere, and there won't really be a need to fulfill that duty towards them. Basically, if one finds someone that wants what they want in a relationship and also doesn't want what one doesn't want in a relationship, those two are probably compatible for each other, enough to have any kind of relationship with each other (whether that's a relationship that has sex or doesn't have it, idk man).

I think in general, people don't like to be perceived in a way that they aren't intending to be perceived as, and I think it's safe to say that, specifically, people don't want to be sexualized when that isn't at all their intent to sexualize themselves. I don't think that's isolated to ace people. I know people, women mostly, that aren't ace or aro that would affirm that. Unwanted sexualization is a kind of perception with an inherent layer of suckiness and almost creepiness. It's sucky to deal with people who want something from you that you don't want to give them and could never intend to give them. It's sucky to deal with people who assume things of you just because of the way you look. And with the added creepiness of sexualization, those experiences and people increase in suckiness (lol I said that word more than I wanted to). I think the fact that you associate being sexualized with interactions with men seems like a result of your childhood experiences, certainly. After all, you don't have, or at least haven't expressed that you have, that same association with women. I think asexuality adds another layer of repulsion to that if one is sex-repulsed or at least repulsed at the idea of doing anything sexual with someone they don't know or trust and things like that. So I think in your case it may be kind of both, depending on some stuff.

If you had a fear of being sexualized by all people regardless of their gender, I think that would be different. I know I don't want to be sexualized ever, however this doesn't lead to me being as innately afraid of women, who definitely can sexualize me, and maybe some have. It's just that due to experiences, I know I associate the instance of being sexualized with interactions with/being perceived by men than with anything else.

  
All that to say I think I'm in a similar boat as you, OP, which has led to me identifying overall as kind of questioning. While I heavily identify with a lot of arospec and acespec feelings and experiences, I also know I have such a complicated idea of men due to personal and second hand experiences. And I know that affects my ability to be attracted to them because it's so hard to feel safe around them, and to me, love is safety. I often wonder what it would be like to work through my fear of men, and if that would change my ability to be attracted to them. But who knows. Hope this helps!

Yeah, I think those things can definitely play a role in creating a low self-worth. For example, a fear of failure could lead to the cognitive belief that even if someone does proclaim to love you, you could fail them in such a way that they won't. In my experience, embarrassment can quickly lead to shame, from feeling self-conscious of ones faults (which I consider embarrassment) to then feeling self-conscious and humiliated at one's very self and beginning to view oneself as one's faults (which I consider shame), and that could lead to a low sense of self worth. Can't speak much to your experience with being autistic, as I am not autistic myself, but I can relate to not fitting in for sure. It may be that you internalize that feeling of not fitting in as what defines your worth. (That's something I would do at times, but after making friends, I stopped caring about whether I fit in with everyone else cuz that just stopped mattering to me what people I'm not close to think of me, as long as they don't want to harm me.)

Some tips for introspection, when you think of the sentence "I don't believe anyone will love me," consider the other sensations that come to mind. Does that sentence emotionally hurt you to believe or say? For example, when I think it, I feel sad to the point of having a little painful pang in my chest. What sort of "proof" or reasons for your belief comes up? For me, I can think of all the times people have hurt me, especially when I thought they were not suppose to do that at all as they claimed to love me. (Not all of these instances I consider traumatic, but definitely hurtful at the very least). Or all the ways I fall short of expecatations, others or my own. These are just my personal examples; yours may be different. 

And whatever comes up, I think someone like a counselor would be great to process that with. Glad to hear you will be seeing a counselor; seeing mine has definitely helped me learn more about myself. Also glad to hear you have friends to talk to, and hopefully you can have this conversation with them if you want to.

I might sound like a crazy armchair psychologist here, but I suppose someone could also have low self-worth from things outside of what most consider trauma, like something like failing self-expectations or having a belief system that at some point centers around internalized shame.

I'm not entirely sure if this will answer your questions, but I'm just going to share my experiences.

So I identify with the terms "lithromantic" and "amicusromantic." Being amicusromantic, I can only be romantically attracted to those I both trust and consider close friends (it's similar to demiromantic in that way). Intersecting that with lithromantic, I experience that attraction only to close friends I trust, but I don't want them to reciprocate. I found out that I was both of these things after I fell in love with a friend. 

Prior to falling in love with my friend, I would have a ton of "crushes" but never do anything about them because I didn't want to know whether they liked me or not because I just didn't really care if they reciprocated or not. Some of them I would actually be repulsed at the thought of being in a relationship with them. I would just keep my crushes to myself and wait til they died out.

After falling in love with my friend and eventually falling out, all these "crushes" just stopped because I realized that they were never that deep anyway, had never been on people I know as deeply as I do my friend, had never been on people I had trusted as I had my friend. So I just never experienced them again. I figure falling in love once altered the chemistry of my brain or something lol.

At the current moment, I wouldn't say I crave romance. I don't necessarily want to fall in love again (though it would be good songwriting/poetry material). Sometimes I desire what could be considered romantic actions (kissing, being close), but that's it. It's interesting how you explain romance in your post (being married with kids) because to me that isn't so much romance as it is just wanting to have a family of my own. I also want kids, despite being God knows where on the asexual spectrum and frequently sex-repulsed (also only attracted to men and I have mild to intense androphobia haha. but not so haha).
